article.headline: Giant blue scorpion - care guide
article.description: A detailed guide to keeping the giant blue scorpion: size, terrarium, substrate, temperature, humidity, diet, venom and moulting.

name: Giant blue scorpion
lead: One of the largest scorpions in the world, with a shell that shows a blue-green sheen under light. Impressive to watch and mildly venomous, but not for handling.
photoAlt: Giant blue scorpion (Heterometrus spinifer) on moist substrate - NS Reptiles Novi Sad
intro: The giant blue scorpion (Heterometrus spinifer) lives in the humid forests of Southeast Asia and is one of the largest scorpions in the world. It owes its name to the blue-green sheen of its dark shell. Its venom is mild, and it relies on its powerful claws more than its sting for defense. With a roomy terrarium, deep moist substrate and occasional feeding with insects, its care is simple - but it is an animal to observe, not to cuddle.

boxes.title: Origin and habitat
p: It comes from Southeast Asia, where it lives on the floor of humid tropical forests. It lives in burrows it digs in the soil, usually under rocks, roots and rotting logs, and is active at night.

boxes.title: Size and appearance
p: Adults reach up to about 12 cm in length, which places it among the largest scorpions in the world. The shell is black but shows a distinct blue-green sheen under light, which gave the species its name. The claws are large and powerful and the body is massive. Species of the genus Heterometrus are very similar to one another and are often mixed up in the trade, but their care is practically the same.

boxes.title: Behavior
p: It hides in its burrow during the day and comes out to hunt after dark. When it feels threatened, it takes a defensive stance with claws and tail raised. Although scorpions of this genus are sometimes kept in groups, there is always a risk that one will eat another, especially during a moult. Keeping them individually is the safest option.

boxes.title: Terrarium
p: A horizontal terrarium is needed, since this scorpion lives on and in the ground and does not climb. For one adult, a terrarium of about 45–60 cm in length is enough. The lid must fit tightly and be secured, and ventilation should be enough to prevent mould, but not so strong that the substrate dries out quickly.

boxes.title: Substrate
p: In the wild it digs burrows, so deep substrate is essential - at least 10–15 cm. A good choice is a mix of coco fiber and fertilizer-free soil, optionally with a little sand or clay so burrows hold their shape. Keep the lower layers moist at all times; the surface can be slightly drier.

boxes.title: Hides and decor
p: Place a piece of cork bark or a half-log on the substrate for the scorpion to start its burrow under. Put heavier decor (rocks, roots) directly on the terrarium floor before adding substrate, so it cannot collapse on the animal while it digs. A few hides and some dry leaves are enough - there is no need to clutter the terrarium.

boxes.title: Temperature
p: During the day about 24–28 °C is ideal, and at night the temperature can drop by a few degrees. If the room is cooler, attach a heat mat to part of a side or back wall of the terrarium, not under the substrate - the scorpion escapes heat by digging down, so heating from below could overheat it.

boxes.title: Humidity and water
p: Air humidity should be around 70–80%. Keep the substrate moist by watering one corner from time to time rather than spraying the animal itself. Provide a shallow dish of clean water and change it every few days.

boxes.title: Lighting and UV light
p: It is nocturnal and needs no special lighting or UVB - daylight from the room is enough, out of direct sun. Like other scorpions, it glows blue-green under a UV lamp (blacklight). This is fascinating to watch, but switch the UV lamp on only briefly, not as permanent lighting. Right after a moult the glow is faint until the new exoskeleton hardens.

boxes.title: Prey
p: It eats only live insects: crickets, roaches (e.g. dubia), locusts and similar prey of a suitable size. The prey should not be larger than the scorpion's body. Do not feed wild-caught insects, as they can carry parasites or pesticides.

boxes.title: Feeding frequency
p: One or two insects a week are enough for an adult, while young scorpions are fed more often and with smaller prey. Remove any insects not eaten within a day - live crickets can stress or even injure the animal, especially during a moult. It is normal for a scorpion to refuse food at times, especially before a moult.

boxes.title: Venom
p: The venom is mild: for most people the sting is comparable to a bee sting - local pain, redness and swelling that pass within a few hours. As with bee stings, an allergic reaction is possible. If breathing difficulties, spreading swelling or nausea develop after a sting, seek medical help immediately.

boxes.title: Claws and defense
p: For defense, the giant blue scorpion relies more on its powerful claws than on its sting. When it feels threatened, it raises its claws and tail, and a pinch can be painful. It is defensive and not a pet to cuddle - it is an animal to observe.

boxes.title: Handling
p: Do not pick it up with bare hands. To move it, use long soft-tipped tongs (tweezers with rubber tips) or guide it into a container and cover it. When cleaning the terrarium, always know where the scorpion is. Keep the terrarium out of reach of children and other pets.

boxes.title: Lifespan
p: With good care it usually lives 5–8 years, although sources give somewhat different figures. It takes several years to reach full size.

boxes.title: Moulting
p: Young scorpions moult several times before they reach adulthood. Before a moult they stop eating and retreat into their burrow. Do not disturb them during this time and do not leave live prey in the terrarium. After a moult the new exoskeleton is soft, so wait about a week before feeding, until it hardens. Moulting goes well only with enough moisture.

boxes.title: Possible problems
p: Most problems are caused by dried-out substrate, mould and leftover food. Failed moults are most often the result of humidity that is too low. Remove dead insects and prey remains regularly. If the scorpion has not eaten for a long time and is not about to moult, or is visibly weak, check the temperature and humidity and see a vet who specializes in exotic animals.

boxes.title: Breeding
p: Females give birth to live young, which they carry on their backs until the first moult. Breeding requires experience and a separate setup; beginners are better off keeping a single scorpion.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about the giant blue scorpion

items.q: Is the giant blue scorpion's sting dangerous?
items.a: For most people it is not - the sting is similar in strength to a bee sting. An allergic reaction is possible, so if breathing difficulties or spreading swelling develop, seek medical help immediately.

items.q: Why is it called the blue scorpion?
items.a: Its dark shell shows a blue-green sheen under light. Under a UV lamp, like other scorpions, it glows blue-green.

items.q: How big does a giant blue scorpion get?
items.a: Adults reach up to about 12 cm in length.

items.q: How long does a giant blue scorpion live?
What does a giant blue scorpion eat?
items.a: Live insects of a suitable size - crickets, roaches and locusts. One or two insects a week are enough for an adult.

items.q: Can I hold a giant blue scorpion?
items.a: We do not recommend it. It is defensive and its claws can give a painful pinch. To move it, use long soft-tipped tongs or a container.
